en: The Sutra on the Five Kings Spoken by the Buddha;
the translator’s name is lost, now appended to the Catalogue of the Eastern Jin.
Formerly there were five kings whose kingdoms were adjacent to one another. They frequented each other’s realms and did not wage war against one another.
He acted solely as a virtuous friend.
His eldest son was named King Puhuan (Universal Peace), who practiced the bodhisattva path;
the other four younger princes constantly practiced unwholesome conduct.

The Great King, out of compassion and wishing to deliver them, summoned them to the palace hall to enjoy themselves together for seven days, performing music and entertainment throughout the day and night.
When the seven days had passed, the Four Kings together addressed the Great King, saying:
"State affairs are many; we pray that you return to govern.
The Great King spoke to his attendants:
"He prepared his carriage and retinue, and the ministers, officials, and citizens all escorted him together.
When they had reached the midpoint of the journey, the Great King, moved by compassion and desiring to deliver them, spoke to the four kings, saying:
"Each of you, speak of the matters for which you long."
One king said: "I wish to obtain the three months of the warm spring, when the trees are in full bloom, so that I may sport in the wilds; this is what I delight in."
Another king spoke again:

"I wish to always be a king, with saddled horses, finery, towers, pavilions, and halls, surrounded on all sides by officials and subjects; resplendent and radiant, with bells struck and drums beaten as I enter and exit, pass and come, while the people on the road turn their eyes toward me—this is my joy."
Another king spoke again:
"My delight is different once more.
I wish for a fine wife and fine sons, peerlessly handsome, with whom I may enjoy myself and indulge my desires to the full; this is my delight."
Another king spoke again:
"My delight is yet different.

I wish that my parents were always present, with many brothers, wives, and children; with fine garments and delicious food arrayed before them so they may satisfy their appetites, and with plain lutes and elegant robes, we might enjoy ourselves together—this is my delight."
When each had finished expressing what they desired, the four kings all turned their heads and said to their great king,
"What is it that you yourself desire? The great king replied:
"I have first spoken of what you all delight in, and then I shall speak of my own delight.
One of you said, 'In the third month of spring, when the trees are in full bloom, we sport in the wilds. Yet in autumn they wither and fall; this is not a lasting joy."

“You alone have said: ‘May I always be a king, surrounded on all sides by saddled horses, finery, towers, pavilions, halls, officials, and subjects; resplendent and dazzling, with bells and drums being struck as I go in and out, causing passersby to turn their eyes toward me. Yet the kings of antiquity, amidst the deep and resonant sounds of their courts and their boundless pleasures, saw their merit and virtue eventually exhausted; nations attacked one another, and they suddenly perished—this was not a lasting joy.”

"You alone have said: 'I wish for a fine wife and fine children, peerless in their beauty, with whom I may enjoy myself and indulge my passions to the utmost. Yet when illness strikes in a single day, the suffering and grief are immeasurable; this is no lasting pleasure."

“You alone have said: ‘I wish that my parents were always present, with many brothers, wives, and children; that fine clothes and delicious foods be arrayed before them to satisfy their appetites, and that we enjoy ourselves together with plain zithers and elegant robes. Yet, should an emergency arise one morning and you be seized by officials, bound and confined in prison without any protection or aid—this is not a lasting joy.”
The four men asked together:
"What does the king delight in? The king said:

"I delight in that which is neither born nor dies, neither suffers nor is afflicted, neither hungry nor thirsty, neither cold nor hot, and wherein existence and non-existence are both mastered; this is my delight."
The four kings spoke together, saying:
"Where is this bliss? Where shall we find a wise teacher?"
The Great King replied, "My teacher is titled 'Buddha' and resides nearby at the Jetavana Monastery.
The various kings rejoiced and each went to the Buddha's location; they all prostrated themselves in salutation and withdrew to sit on one side.
The Great King knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“We who have now obtained this human form are dull-witted, ignorant, and lacking in wisdom; we are merely deeply attached to worldly pleasures and do not understand the nature of sin and merit.”
"I pray that the Buddha will explain the Truth of Suffering for the sake of us disciples.
The Buddha said:
"Listen well, all of you!"
I shall now speak for you.

Throughout their lives in this world, human beings are constantly beset by immeasurable sufferings that pierce the very core of their being; for your sake, I shall now briefly explain these eight types of suffering.
What are the eight sufferings?

The suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of separation from what is loved, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, the suffering of encountering what is hated, and the suffering of grief, lamentation, pain, and despair.
These are the eight sufferings.
What is meant by the suffering of birth?

When a person dies, they do not know toward which realm the spirit is heading; before a place of rebirth is obtained, they assume the form of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). Upon reaching the twenty-first day, when the parents unite, the spirit comes to receive conception in the womb.
In the first week, it is like thin curd;
in the second week, it is like thick curd;
in the third week, it is like solidified butter.

In the fourth week, it is like a piece of raw flesh; in the fifth week, blisters form. When the *vāyu* (wind) enters the womb skillfully, it blows upon the body, causing the six sense organs (*ṣaḍāyatana*) to open.

While within the mother’s womb—situated below the stomach (*āmāśaya*) and above the large intestine (*pakvāśaya*)—if the mother eats a cup of hot food, it drenches the fetus's body as if entering a cauldron of boiling water;
if the mother drinks a cup of cold water, it feels as if ice is cutting into its body.
When the mother is full, her body is constricted by the fetus, causing an unspeakable pain;
when the mother is hungry, there is a gnawing sensation within her belly, as if she were being hung upside down, and she suffers immeasurably.
When the full moon arrives and he is about to be born, his head turns toward the birth canal with a pain as intense as two boulders squeezing a mountain;
at the moment of birth, the mother is in peril and the father is filled with dread.
Born and falling upon the grass, his body is delicate and soft; when the grass touches his body, it is as if he were treading upon swords and blades, and he suddenly lets out a piercing cry.
Is this suffering or not?
The people all said, “This is a great suffering. [The Buddha asked:
“What is meant by the suffering of old age?”

Rearing and nurturing them until they reach adulthood, [the parents] assume they are strong and healthy; they carry light and heavy burdens without self-restraint, enduring extreme cold in winter, extreme heat in summer, extreme hunger when starving, and extreme satiety when full, lacking all moderation.

Gradually they grow old, their heads turn white and teeth fall out; their vision blurs and their hearing grows dull. Vigor departs and decay arrives: the skin slackens, the face wrinkles, the hundred joints ache, walking becomes excruciating, and rising or sitting is done with groaning. Their minds are troubled by sorrow and grief, their consciousness fades, and they forget immediately what has been said; as their life draws to its end, they weep at the mention of it, requiring others' assistance for every movement.
"Is this suffering? The Great King replied,
"It is indeed great suffering."
"What is meant by the suffering of illness?
A person has four great elements (*mahābhūta*) which, in combination, constitute their body. What are these four great elements?

They are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element. If one of these elements becomes unbalanced, one hundred and one illnesses arise; if all four elements become unbalanced, four hundred and four illnesses manifest simultaneously."
When the earth element is disturbed, the entire body feels heavy;
when the water element is disturbed, the entire body becomes swollen;
when the fire element is disturbed, the entire body experiences a burning heat.
When the wind element is disturbed, the entire body becomes rigid and stiff, and the hundred joints ache as if struck by a scourge.

As the four great elements fluctuate, the hands and feet become useless; one’s vital strength is utterly exhausted, and one requires assistance to sit or rise. The mouth becomes parched and the lips wither; the tendons seem to snap and the nose splits open. One no longer sees forms with the eyes nor hears sounds with the ears; impurities flow forth, and the body lies upon them. The mind harbors bitter distress, and every word uttered is filled with sorrow. Though six relatives stay by one's side, watching and tending day and night without ceasing, even sweet delicacies and fine foods taste only of bitterness once they enter the mouth.
"Is this suffering? He replied,
"It is indeed great suffering."
"What is the suffering of death?
When a person dies, four hundred and four ailments arise simultaneously; the four great elements seek to disperse, and the soul and spirit are unsettled."

At the moment of death, the "sword-wind" (kṣuraka-vāyu) dissolves the physical form; there is no part of the body that does not ache, as white sweat flows forth and both hands grope through empty space.
Family members, both inside and outside the room, stand at his side, weeping in grief and sorrow; their pain pierces to the very marrow of their bones, such that they cannot endure it.
When death occurs, the wind-element departs and the vital breath ceases; the fire-element is extinguished and the body grows cold, with the wind departing first and the fire following.
The soul departs, and the body becomes rigid and straight, no longer possessing any consciousness.

Within ten days, the flesh rotted and blood flowed; it became bloated, putrid, and foul-smelling beyond description. It was cast away into the wilderness, where flocks of birds devoured it until the flesh was gone and the bones were bleached dry; the skulls lay scattered in different places.
"Is this suffering? He replied,
"It is indeed great suffering."
"What is meant by the suffering of separation from those one loves?

Within the four walls of a household, brothers, wives, and children are bound together in mutual affection. Yet in a single morning they may be ruined and scattered, plundered by others; father to the east and son to the west, mother to the south and daughter to the north. No longer remaining in one place, they become slaves to others, each wailing in grief as their hearts break within. Enveloped in profound darkness, there is no hope of ever seeing one another again."
"Is this suffering? He replied,
"It is indeed great suffering."
"What is the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks?

A man has wealth and money at home, yet he squanders it and pursues high office. The officials and commoners hope to attain riches and honor; they toil and strive to seek it, seeking without ceasing. Eventually, they happen to obtain it and become a district magistrate on the frontier."

Before long, having greedily seized the property of the people, he was denounced by others; one morning, when trouble arose, he was taken away in a cangue-cart. As he was about to be executed, his grief and suffering were immeasurable, for he knew not on what day he would live or die.
"Is this suffering? He replied,
"It is indeed great suffering."
"What is meant by the suffering of association with the disliked? In this world, people are base and vulgar;

dwelling together amidst love and desire, they contend over trivial matters, eventually harming one another until they become great enemies. They avoid each other, finding no place to hide; each sharpens their blades and notches their arrows, clutching bows and holding staves, terrified at the mere thought of meeting. When they encounter one another on a narrow path, each draws their bow and looses their arrows, two swords facing each other, not knowing who will emerge victorious. At such a time, the fear is immeasurable."
"Is this suffering? He replied,
"It is indeed great suffering."
"What is meant by sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering?
When humans are born into this world, those with long lives may reach a hundred years, while those with short lives perish in the womb or are miscarried."
As for those who live long lives, even if they reach a hundred years, half is consumed by night; thus fifty years remain.
Furthermore, five years are subtracted for being intoxicated or afflicted by disease and failing to act as a human being, and the period of childhood is spent in folly.
For fifteen years, I did not know the rules of propriety;
now that I am over eighty, I am old, dull, and without wisdom—my ears are deaf and my eyes are dim—and I lack all sense of dharma for another twenty years.
Thus, at ninety, with ten more years remaining, I have been burdened by much sorrow—O Deva!
He grieves when there is sexual disorder below; he grieves when there is drought in the world; he grieves when there is great flooding in the world;
he grieves when there is heavy frost in the world; he grieves when there is no harvest in the world; he grieves when there are many ailments and illnesses within his household;
he grieves over maintaining his wealth and property and fears losing his livelihood; he grieves over the hundreds of [taxes] from the government...
He is anxious when his debts are not yet repaid; he is anxious when family members encounter legal trouble with the local authorities and are imprisoned, with no known date for their release;
he is anxious when brothers, wives, or children have traveled far and have not yet returned; he is anxious when his household is impoverished and cold, lacking food and clothing;
he is anxious when neighbors or the village encounters trouble; and he is anxious when the community sacrificial offerings cannot be prepared.
Furthermore, he grieves when members of his household die and he lacks the means for their coffining and burial;
he also grieves when spring arrives and he has no oxen for plowing— thus, with such various sorrows and lamentations, there is never a time of joy.
"When we gather together on this festival day, instead of rejoicing, we instead shed tears toward one another.
Is this not suffering? He replied:
"This is indeed great suffering.

At that time, the five kings, their various ministers, and several tens of millions of people in the assembly, upon hearing the exposition of the Truths of Suffering, had their minds opened and their understanding awakened; they immediately attained the stage of *srotāpanna*. All were filled with great joy, paid their respects, and departed.
The Four Kings together addressed King Puhuan, saying:
"Great King, you are truly a Bodhisattva of great power; by transforming us and speaking to us, you have enabled us to attain the traces of the Path—this is the grace of the Great King."

"In the past, when I contemplated these palaces, my mind was filled with attachment and I could not distance myself from them; now, beholding these palaces, I see them as if looking upon a foul latrine—there is nothing in them to be desired."
He immediately abdicated the throne to his younger brother, left the household life to pursue the Way, and cultivated all manner of meritorious virtues without weariness day after day.
This is the *Sūtra on the Five Kings* spoken by the Buddha.
